# Phantasia as the Soul's Temporal Medium: Motion, Time, and the Genesis of Phantasmata

## I. Introduction: Phantasia as the Soul's Temporal Medium

The question of phantasia — what it is, how it functions, and why Aristotle accords it such a pivotal role in the architecture of the soul — has long remained one of the most contested topics in Aristotelian scholarship. Indeed, the difficulty arises not merely from the semantic breadth of the term, which resists any simple translation into "imagination" or "mental imagery," but from the structural position phantasia occupies between perception (aisthesis) and thought (noesis), between the body's reception of sensible form and the soul's capacity to deliberate, judge, and act. 24). Thus phantasia is neither a mere residue of sensation nor an autonomous cognitive act; it is, rather, the mediating power through which sensory motion persists, transforms, and becomes available for higher-order operations of the soul. To understand phantasia adequately, we must situate it within the broader ontological framework of motion and time — the very conditions under which anything can appear, endure, and recur within the soul's experience. This chapter proposes a temporal reading of phantasia, one that traces its genesis through a sequence of ontological moments we designate T0 through T3. At T0, motion and time constitute the irreducible horizon within which all being and becoming unfold; at T1, the soul receives the first motion of perception, the pure affection of aisthesis; at T2, the residual motion that persists after the sensible object has departed generates an intermediate kinetic trace; and at T3, this trace crystallizes into the phantasma proper, a dual inscription of resonant motion and resonant affect. The temporal framework is not imposed externally upon Aristotle's account but is drawn from his own insistence, in the *Physics*, that time is the "number of motion in respect of the before and after" and that all change is intelligible only within the continuum of temporal succession (Aristotle, *Physics*, p. 39). Specifically, the movement from T0 to T3 represents not a series of discrete instants but a continuous unfolding in which each stage is the necessary condition for the next, much as Heidegger's analysis of temporality reveals Dasein's Being as always already stretched along between past, present, and future (Heidegger, *Being and Time*, p. 499). What distinguishes phantasia from aisthesis on the one hand and noesis on the other is precisely its temporal character — its capacity to hold and reproduce what is no longer present, to make the absent sensorially available. Phantasia is not a mixture of sensation and judgment, as Plato believed, but a distinct faculty rooted in the soul's kinetic constitution. As Papachristou has demonstrated, a careful reading of *De Anima* reveals that Aristotle discriminates not merely two but "three kinds or grades of phantasia: (a) Indefinite/indeterminate phantasia (ἀόριστος φαντασία)" and further grades connected to perception and deliberation respectively (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 25–27). The internal distinctions among sensory phantasia, which humans share with other animals, and deliberative or bouleutike phantasia, which belongs to rational beings alone, will be examined in detail in Chapter IV; here we note only that these grades correspond to different temporal depths of the phantasma's formation, ranging from the near-immediate afterimage to the complex deliberative image that informs practical reasoning. Similarly, the relation between phantasia and belief (doxa) — a relation Aristotle carefully circumscribes — and the question of phantasia's voluntariness, its susceptibility to being summoned at will, will receive sustained treatment in subsequent chapters. For now, it suffices to establish the ontological ground: phantasia is the soul's temporal medium, the faculty through which motion becomes memory, and memory becomes the material of thought. ## II. T0–T3: Motion, Time, and the Genesis of Phantasmata

Before we can analyze the individual stages of phantasmatic genesis, we must grasp the overarching logic that binds them into a coherent sequence. The movement from T0 to T3 is not a mechanical process of information transfer but an ontological unfolding in which the soul's capacity for being-affected (paschein) generates progressively more complex forms of kinetic presence. Aristotle's account of motion in the *Physics* provides the foundational grammar for this process: motion is the actuality of the potential qua potential, the passage from what something can be to what it is becoming (Aristotle, *Physics*, p. 39). Accordingly, each transition from one temporal moment to the next is itself a motion — a further actualization of a capacity that was latent in the preceding stage. At T0, the world moves, and time measures that movement; at T1, the soul is moved by the sensible object; at T2, the soul continues to be moved even after the object's departure; at T3, this continuing motion crystallizes into a phantasma that bears both a kinetic trace and an affective valence. The philosophical challenge here is (Aristotle 2014) a motion that begins outside the soul — in the physical alteration of the sensory medium — comes to reside within the soul as an enduring image possessed of qualitative character. This is, in essence, the problem of emergence: how do novel properties arise from the interaction of lower-level components? 7–8). The parallel with Aristotle's account is striking; the phantasma is an emergent property of the soul's kinetic system, arising from the complex interaction of sensory reception, residual motion, and the soul's own affective disposition. Thus the T0–T3 framework captures not merely a temporal sequence but an ontological stratification, each level of which introduces properties that cannot be reduced to those of the preceding level. Heidegger's existential analytic provides an additional lens through which to view this stratification. In *Being and Time*, temporality is not simply one feature of Dasein's existence among others; it is the "temporal way of describing this phenomenon" that discloses Dasein's Being as fundamentally stretched along the ecstatic horizons of past, present, and future (Heidegger, *Being and Time*, p. 499). When we apply this insight to Aristotle's account of phantasia, we see that the phantasma is not merely an image that happens to occur in time but is itself a temporal structure — a holding-present of what has passed, a making-available of what might yet come. Burke's dramatistic method similarly attends to the reduction of complexity into "summarizing" terms; (Hawhee 2011), when confronting any motive-term that presents itself as simple, "we must forthwith ask ourselves what complexities are subsumed beneath it" (Burke, *A Grammar of Motives*, pp. 126–127). The phantasma, seemingly a simple image, subsumes within itself the complexity of an entire kinetic and temporal history. The sections that follow trace this history from its origin in motion and time (T0) through its culmination in the dual trace of the phantasma (T3). ## II.1 T0 — Motion and Time as Ontological Horizon

The ontological horizon within which phantasia becomes possible is constituted by motion (kinesis) and time (chronos). For Aristotle, motion is the most fundamental category of becoming; it is the actuality of what exists potentially insofar as it exists potentially, and it pervades every domain of natural existence. In the *Physics*, Aristotle insists that the infinite itself — the boundless continuum within which motion unfolds — "has this mode of existence: one thing is always being taken after another, and each thing that is taken is always finite, but always different" (Aristotle, *Physics*, pp. 39–40). This characterization is crucial for understanding the temporal medium of phantasia, because it establishes that the continuum of motion is not a static substrate but a perpetual process of succession, each moment giving way to the next in an unbroken flow. Time, as the number of this motion with respect to before and after, is accordingly not a container within which events occur but the very measure of their occurrence — the articulation of the "before" and "after" that makes any succession intelligible. Bowin's analysis of Aristotle's account of time perception reinforces this point. As Bowin observes, "Aristotle clearly says that the now 'divides potentially' (Phys. 4.13.222a14)" and that nows exist potentially prior to being marked off by a perceiving soul (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, pp. 4–5). The now is not a fixed boundary but a potential division within the continuous flow of time, actualized only when a soul attends to the transition from one phase of motion to another. Hence, even at the most fundamental level — the level of T0, before any particular sensation has occurred — the conditions for phantasia are already in place, because time itself requires a soul capable of marking the now, and this marking is already a proto-perceptual act. The soul does not stand outside time and then enter it through perception; rather, the soul is always already within the temporal continuum, attuned to the motion that constitutes the world's becoming. Heidegger's reading of Greek ontology extends this insight by showing that Being, for the Greeks, is fundamentally understood as presence (Anwesenheit), the coming-to-presence of what is within the horizon of time. 499). What Heidegger suggests is that the Greeks' understanding of Being as temporal presence already implies a perceptual subject for whom things appear — a subject whose encounter with the world is structured by the before and after of temporal succession. At T0, then, we have not merely physical motion and its temporal measure but the ontological readiness of the soul to receive the motions of the world. Aristotle's account in *Sense and Sensibilia* of how sensory media transmit motion between object and organ presupposes this readiness; specifically, the parts of the medium between a sensory organ and its object are affected in a sequential manner that mirrors the temporal structure of motion itself (Aristotle, *Sense and Sensibilia*, pp. 19–20). The medium's sequential affection is the physical counterpart of the soul's temporal receptivity, and together they constitute the horizon — T0 — within which phantasia will subsequently emerge. ## II.2 T1 — Aisthesis: First Motion and Pure Reception

At T1, the ontological horizon of motion and time becomes concretely actualized in the event of aisthesis — the soul's first reception of sensory motion from an external object. This is the moment at which the world impresses itself upon the soul, not by transferring matter but by communicating form through the sensory medium. Aristotle's account in *Sense and Sensibilia* makes clear that perception involves a genuine motion, an alteration of the sense organ by the sensible quality of the object; indeed, "the parts of media between a sensory organ and its object are not all affected at once — except in the case of light" (Aristotle, *Sense and Sensibilia*, pp. 19–20). The sequential character of this affection is significant: it means that even the first moment of perception unfolds in time, that reception is itself a temporal process rather than an instantaneous event. The soul at T1 is not merely passive in the sense of being inert; it is rather receptive in the sense of being ontologically prepared — attuned, in Heidegger's vocabulary — to receive the motion that the medium communicates. Heidegger's analysis of Dasein's thrownness (Geworfenheit) provides a structural parallel to this moment of pure reception. Dasein does not choose its attunement to the world; it finds itself always already disposed in a particular way, affected by what it encounters before any reflective act of judgment. Similarly, aisthesis at T1 is pre-reflective and pre-judgmental; it is the soul's being-affected by the world prior to any interpretive overlay. This is why Aristotle insists that phantasia is distinct from both perception and judgment: perception gives us the first motion, judgment evaluates it, but phantasia occupies the interval between them, holding the motion in a form that is neither raw sensation nor conceptual thought. Subsequently, the motion received at T1 does not simply vanish when the external object is removed; it persists as a residual kinetic trace, a continuing vibration within the soul's sensory apparatus. This persistence is the key to the transition from T1 to T2, and it is what distinguishes the living soul from a merely physical medium that ceases to be affected once the stimulus is withdrawn. Rickert's concept of ambient rhetoric illuminates a further dimension of T1. 57–60). Similarly, aisthesis at T1 is not a merely internal event but an ecological encounter in which the soul and the world interpenetrate through the medium of sensory motion. 7–8). At T1, the complex configuration is the intersection of sensory organ, medium, and sensible object; the emergent state is the perceptual act itself, irreducible to any of its physical components taken in isolation. Thus T1 marks the genesis of experiential life — the moment at which mere physical motion becomes the soul's lived encounter with the world. ## II.3 T2 — Residual Motion and Apoleipomene Kinesis

The transition from T1 to T2 is marked by a phenomenon that Aristotle terms apoleipomene kinesis — the residual or "left-behind" motion that persists in the sensory apparatus after the external object has been removed. This concept is central to Aristotle's account of afterimages, dreams, and the broader phenomenon of phantasia, because (White 1985) the soul can entertain appearances in the absence of the objects that originally caused them. In *Sense and Sensibilia*, Aristotle provides a vivid illustration of this residual motion: the phenomenon of visual persistence, in which an image lingers after one has looked at a bright object, occurs because the motion imparted to the sense organ continues to propagate even when the stimulus ceases. As Aristotle notes, "the phenomenon does not occur unless the motion is rapid and takes place in darkness" (Aristotle, *Sense and Sensibilia*, pp. 5–6). The conditions he specifies — rapidity and darkness — reveal that residual motion is not a marginal epiphenomenon but a lawful consequence of the kinetic nature of perception; when the external stimulus is strong enough and subsequent stimulation is minimized, the persisting motion becomes perceptible in its own right. What is philosophically significant about T2 is that it represents a moment of ontological ambiguity: the soul is moved, but not by an external object currently present; it is affected, but the affection is a trace rather than a direct impression. This ambiguity is precisely what makes phantasia possible and also what makes it susceptible to error — for the soul may take a residual motion for a fresh perception, or may confuse the trace of one object with the presence of another. The motion at T2, in Aristotle's terms, exists in an intermediate mode; it is neither the full actuality of aisthesis nor the complete absence of motion, but rather a potentiality that persists in the sense organ and in the common sense. Indeed, Aristotle's broader account of perceptual thresholds in *Sense and Sensibilia* supports this reading; (Hawhee 2011) "the increment of sense-perception is not perceptible in itself, nor capable of separate existence (since it exists only potentially in the more distinctly perceivable whole of sense-perception)" (Aristotle, *Sense and Sensibilia*, pp. 17–18). The residual motion at T2 similarly exists in a potential mode — it is part of the perceptual whole without being distinctly perceivable as a separate entity. Gibson's ecological approach to perception provides a complementary framework for understanding T2. Gibson insists that perception is not a matter of constructing internal representations from discrete sensory inputs but of picking up information directly from the structured ambient array. (Hawhee 2011) "the events we are concerned with are 'external,' so a displacement of the point of observation will be excluded, because it refers to the locomotion of a potential observer, not to the motion of a surface" (Gibson, *The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception*, pp. 116–117). While Gibson's framework is explicitly anti-representational, his emphasis on the persistence and structure of the ambient array helps to illuminate why Aristotle's residual motion is not merely a neural afterglow but a structured kinetic event. The motion that persists at T2 retains something of the informational structure of the original perception; it is not random noise but a patterned residue that preserves, however imperfectly, the formal character of the sensible object. Hence, the transition from T2 to T3 is not a leap from chaos to order but a further articulation of a kinetic pattern that was already nascent in the moment of original reception. Accordingly, T2 serves as the crucial intermediate stage at which the raw motion of aisthesis begins its transformation into the complex, form-bearing phantasma. ## II.4 T3 — Phantasmata and the Dual Trace: Resonant Motion and Resonant Affect

At T3, the residual motion of T2 crystallizes into the phantasma proper — an internal appearance that bears a dual character, being at once a kinetic trace (a persisting pattern of motion in the soul's sensory apparatus) and an affective inscription (a qualitative coloring that disposes the soul toward pursuit or avoidance, desire or aversion). The concept of a dual trace is essential because it captures what is distinctive about phantasmata as opposed to mere afterimages or mechanical reverberations: the phantasma is not only a motion but a motion that matters, a motion that carries with it the soul's affective response to the original object. Gonzalez's reading of Aristotle's *De Anima* underscores this point; (Hawhee 2011) "the movers of the animal are reasoning and phantasia and choice and wish and appetite" (Gonzalez, *The Meaning and Function of Phantasia in Aristotle's 'Rhetoric' III.1*, pp. 24–25). Phantasia thus stands at the intersection of cognition and desire; the phantasma is not merely an image to be contemplated but an appearance that moves the soul toward action. The emergence of this dual trace at T3 can be understood through O'Connor and Wong's diachronic model of emergence. On their account, "E at t1 will help to determine the physical state of S at the subsequent moment, t2, but presumably not its continuing to exhibit P*" and "E, we may suppose, will also help to determine the occurrence at t2 of another emergent state, E2" (O'Connor and Wong, *The Metaphysics of Emergence*, pp. 9–10). Translating this into Aristotelian terms: the emergent perceptual state at T1 (the first motion of aisthesis) generates a residual kinetic trace at T2 that in turn gives rise to a further emergent state at T3 — the phantasma, which is irreducible to the physical motion that underlies it because it possesses qualitative and affective properties not present in the mere vibration of the sense organ. The phantasma at T3 is thus a genuinely novel ontological entity, one that emerges from the soul's kinetic history but cannot be fully explained by any single stage of that history taken in isolation. The diachronic variety of emergence, in which an emergent property at one moment is "partly causally determinative" of subsequent physical and mental states (O'Connor and Wong, *The Metaphysics of Emergence*, pp. 11–12), captures the way in which phantasmata at T3 feed forward into deliberation, memory, and action. Aristotle's own account in the *Physics* of how substances retain their identity through change provides a further gloss on the dual trace. (Hawhee 2011) "when a thing has been affected and altered in any way we still call it by the original name: thus we speak of the bronze or the wax being is fluid or hard or hot (not only that — we also call the fluid and the hot stuff bronze), giving the matter the same name as the affection" (Aristotle, *Physics*, p. 100). The analogy to the phantasma is instructive: just as the bronze retains its name even when it has been melted and reshaped, the phantasma retains the formal imprint of the original sensible object even as it has been transformed by the processes of residual motion and affective coloring. The dual trace is thus not a composite of two separate elements glued together but a single ontological structure in which kinetic pattern and affective quality are inseparably intertwined — much as the bronze is at once a substance and a bearer of its current affection. Hawhee's work on Aristotle's rhetorical vision further illuminates this duality;  when Aristotle discusses the epideictic function of lofty language, the term megethos invokes both physical stature and qualitative greatness, a doubling  phantasma's own dual character as both kinetic magnitude and affective significance (Hawhee, *Looking Into Aristotle's Eyes*, pp. 12–13). Finally, the emergence of phantasmata at T3 establishes the conditions for all subsequent operations of the soul — memory, deliberation, desire, and action. The phantasma is the medium through which the past persists into the present and the present is projected into the future; it is, in the fullest sense, the soul's temporal medium. Aristotle's primary substance, the unmoved mover, "produces the primary eternal and single movement" (Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, pp. 146–147); by analogy, the phantasma, once formed, produces within the soul a continuing movement that organizes experience, motivates action, and makes thought possible. Thus the T0–T3 framework reveals phantasia not as a marginal psychological curiosity but as the foundational faculty through which the soul inhabits time — receiving, retaining, and transforming the motions of the world into the appearances that constitute its inner life. The deliberative and rational grades of phantasia, which Aristotle distinguishes as bouleutike phantasia in rational beings (Gonzalez, *The Meaning and Function of Phantasia in Aristotle's 'Rhetoric' III.1*, pp. 22–23), represent further elaborations of this temporal medium, articulations that presuppose the kinetic and affective ground we have traced from T0 to T3. Accordingly, the analysis developed in this chapter provides the necessary foundation for the investigations that follow, in which the phantasma's role in memory, rhetoric, and practical deliberation will be examined in their full complexity. ---
